v.why: Under standard parameterization Adam's function change grows with fan-in, so widening at an already high learning rate pushes training into divergence or dead-ReLU collapse.
With sklearn-style L2 scaled by batch size and applied every minibatch, tiny batches multiply the effective per-epoch shrinkage so an alpha increase causes severe over-regularization.
L2 shrinkage compounds multiplicatively across three weight matrices and collapses signal propagation through the ReLU stack.
At high learning rates each added layer compounds update-induced instability and ReLU death, turning an expressivity gain into an optimization failure.
Narrow nets have a small effective function step per Adam update, so a higher learning rate compensates for their slow progress before instability sets in.
At depth 3 capacity is already supplied by composition, so extra width yields diminishing returns and more parameters to overfit.
Stacking 16-40-unit ReLU layers compounds information loss from dead units, so going deeper hurts narrow nets more than wide ones.
Large batches over a fixed number of epochs give few, low-noise update steps, so a higher learning rate is needed to make progress and is less likely to destabilize.
Wider nets can fit the data with a smaller per-weight norm, so under strong L2 extra width restores expressivity the penalty removes.

When the learning rate is already tiny, enlarging the batch cuts the number of updates in the fixed epoch budget and deepens underfitting, whereas at higher rates fewer steps are harmless or stabilizing.
